title: daemon: run gates in the background so a 60-min gate no longer freezes dispatch, reviews and merges
spec:
Root cause of the 2026-10-07/08 stalls (Planner, 05:20): orchestrator/daemon.py gate() (line 1435) loops over done
execute tasks and calls gate.run_gate(...) synchronously (line ~1491) inside tick(). A Deskmere iOS gate runs 40-60 min and an
orchestrator full gate 20-45 min under load, so the whole tick blocks: dispatch, steering, merge_reviewed and planner_runs
do not run until the gate returns. Observed: luna T-0618/T-0611/T-0612 eligible (daemon.eligible returned them) but not
dispatched for 40+ min while the daemon ran T-0616's gate; ai-apprentice idle for hours the same way.
Fix:
1. gate() starts each gate in a background worker (thread or subprocess via the existing spawn_async pattern) and stamps
   pipeline.gated_at (lease) immediately; the result is posted when the run ends (same status/hold logic as today:
   green -> reviews/merge path, red -> gate_red hold, timeout -> gate_timeout hold, infra failure as today).
2. Concurrency: [gate].max_parallel in pool.toml (default 1, so behaviour is serial but non-blocking); a repo may set 2.
   Never two gates on the same worktree. A daemon restart reconciles gated_at leases without a live gate (re-gate).
3. tick() returns within seconds while a gate runs; dispatch and merges keep working.
4. Keep the bus lock out of the gate run (no bus.locked() or open write transaction across the subprocess).
Tests (tests/test_daemon.py): test_gate_runs_in_background_and_tick_returns, test_gate_result_posted_when_run_ends
(green, red, timeout), test_gate_max_parallel_respected, test_restart_regates_orphaned_gate_lease.
Run: PYTHONPATH=tests uv run python -m unittest tests.test_daemon tests.test_gate_timeout. Commit on the task branch.
acceptance: tick() returns within 5 s while a gate is running
gate results post as before (green, red, timeout)
orphaned gate leases re-gate after a restart

spec_review_risks.issue: Stamping gated_at at gate start collides with how gated_at is used today. It currently means 'gate finished, reviews or merge stamped'. Other code treats it as gated: the dependent 'imminent' check (~887), inflight_claude_dispatches (~510), running-set filtering (~860), merge_pressure.py:95, speculation.py:218/221, duration.py:33 and the scorecards. A running gate would make dependents look gated or merge-ready, and would skew duration and scorecard data. The spec gives no way to tell a gate in flight from a gate finished.

sweep_leases already handles expired gated_at leases, and it reads pipeline['reviews_expected'] unconditionally. A start-time stamp has no reviews_expected, so an expired lease for a live or orphaned gate raises KeyError. If it were fixed to re-gate instead, it would also have to check for a live gate worker. A live gate often outlives the 900 s STAGE_LEASE_S, since gates run 20-60 min. The sweep would then take the already_merged, merge or _open_reviews path, or re-gate in parallel, while the first gate is still running. The spec says leases are 'reconciled' but does not name this branch, and sweep_leases is not mentioned at all.

stamp() returns False when the stage is already set, and the current tail of gate() relies on stamp(gated_at, ...) at completion (held, red, timeout, green). If start-time stamping uses the same key, every completion stamp fails and results are silently dropped. The spec needs a separate in-flight marker (for example pipeline.gate_started_at plus lease), or clear_stage followed by stamp, and a rule for which one marks completion. The 'results post as before' criterion cannot be met otherwise.

No code path is named for tracking live gates. The spec does not say how gate() knows which gates are running (in-process registry or bus fields), how 'never two gates on the same worktree' is enforced, or how max_parallel is counted when the daemon restarts. An in-memory set that is never cleared when a worker raises would leak a slot and stop gating for good. The worker needs try/finally release, and it needs to hold_failed on exceptions, as the current inline code does (hold_failed 'gated_error').

The pre-gate work (gate_attempts increment, dirty check, already_merged git call, acceptance.missing_tests) and the whole post-gate tail (merged_into check, _hold_stale_high, _record_stale_check, _stale_rebase, report_merge/merge.merge, _open_reviews) are slow or git-heavy. The spec does not say which side of the thread boundary they run on. If the whole body goes into the worker, merge.merge and rebase run concurrently with tick()'s merge_reviewed and dispatch, with no serialization against them. Keep gate subprocess in the thread and post results from a tick-side reaper, or state clearly that the tail runs under bus.locked/merge serialization. Also, gate_attempts is bumped on each tick, so a task skipped for max_parallel would inflate it.

Acceptance 'tick() returns within 5 s' is a wall-clock bound, a pattern already flaky in this repo (T-1710 replaced it with an event-based check). The test should block run_gate on a threading.Event and assert tick returns while it is blocked, then release it and join. Result-posting tests also need a deterministic join (the thread, or a reaper called by the test) rather than sleeps. The 'timeout' case must cover the double-timeout hold with gate_timeouts accounting, as today.

gate.run_gate and gate.settings are patched onto the gate function object, and existing tests patch daemon.gate.run_gate. Any restructuring (a worker function, a new registry) must keep that seam and its call signature, or tests in test_daemon and test_gate_timeout will break with no clear cause. test_gate_timeout is in scope but the spec gives no reason for touching it.

[gate].max_parallel is a new config key, but pool.toml is not in scope, and gate.settings() in gate.py is said to own the [gate] defaults. The spec should say that the default lives in code (gate.settings) and that no pool.toml edit is required. It also needs a bound check (>=1, int), since 0 or a bad value would silently stop all gating. There is no rollback story, such as a way to restore serial in-line behaviour.
